questions.q: What is the key difference between an Index Seek and an Index Scan?
options: They are two names for exactly the same operation
A Seek navigates directly to matching rows via the index's B-tree; a Scan reads the entire index top to bottom checking every row
A Seek only works on clustered indexes, a Scan only on nonclustered
A Scan is always faster than a Seek
questions.explain: An unexpected scan on a large table for a selective query is a strong signal the right index doesn't exist or isn't being used.

questions.q: What is a Key Lookup (or RID Lookup)?
options: A second trip back to the clustered index (or heap) to fetch columns that the nonclustered index used for the seek doesn't cover
A type of index that replaces the need for a clustered index
The first step the optimizer always performs, before any seek or scan
An error that means the query failed
questions.explain: At scale, thousands of Key Lookups mean thousands of extra random-I/O trips -- often fixed with an included column turning the index into a covering index.

questions.q: Why does WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 often force a scan even if an index on OrderDate exists?
options: Wrapping the column in a function makes the predicate non-SARGable -- the optimizer would have to evaluate the function for every row before it could match, so it can't use a seek
This always produces a syntax error
Indexes on date columns are never usable in WHERE clauses
YEAR() is not a valid T-SQL function
questions.explain: Rewriting as a direct range comparison on OrderDate (not wrapped in a function) restores SARGability and the possibility of a seek.

questions.q: What does the Hash Match operator do, and what's a risk it carries?
options: It builds an in-memory hash table from one input and probes it with the other -- it can spill to tempdb if the hash table doesn't fit in memory
It never appears in join queries
It is only used for INSERT statements
It always sorts both inputs first, guaranteeing no memory use
questions.explain: Hash Match is common for joins on large, unsorted inputs without a useful index.

questions.q: Which combination of operators is described as the single most common 'add this index' fix in real DBA work?
options: A Sort followed by a Compute Scalar
A Nested Loops join with no other operators
Two consecutive Index Scans on the same table
An Index Seek immediately followed by a Key Lookup on a query returning thousands of rows
questions.explain: The seek itself is fine; the index just doesn't cover enough columns to avoid the second trip -- adding an included column usually fixes it.
